target_search_intent: Find time tracking tools that still produce a usable record when the user forgets to start, stop, or switch timers in real time.
Avoid time tracking tools whose core workflow depends on repeated manual timer initiation throughout the day.
page_identity.user_problem: The user wants time tracking that stays trustworthy even on messy, interrupt-driven days when remembering every timer start, stop, or task switch is unrealistic.
page_identity.dominant_failure_mechanism: The tool fails when trustworthy time records depend on repeated deliberate timer starts, stops, or task switches in the moment, so one missed initiation creates gaps that must be reconstructed later.

mechanism_contract.exact_failure_trigger: Normal time capture depends on the user deliberately starting, stopping, or switching a timer for each work block, and missing one of those initiation actions weakens the timeline enough that the user must reconstruct what happened later.
what_must_be_true: The claimed survivor must preserve a reconstructable timeline without requiring per-task timer initiation in normal use.
The claimed failure must break specifically because real-time initiation is easy to miss, not merely because the tool has extra features, reporting overhead, or setup friction.
A mixed-mode tool can only be named confidently if current evidence shows which mode is normal, primary, or outcome-dominant for this constraint.
what_does_not_count: Manual timesheet entry after the fact, by itself, does not satisfy the survivor mechanism.
Idle reminders, timer reminders, or easier start buttons do not remove manual-timer dependence if the record still depends on remembering to initiate tracking.
A tool being fast, simple, or good for billing does not prove it works without manual timers.

Automatic activity capture that still requires the user to manually convert raw activity into project time may reduce pain, but it is not automatically equivalent to a full survivor unless the page states that narrower behavior precisely.
adjacent_mechanisms_to_exclude: ceiling_check unless the cited comparison explicitly turns on manual-vs-automatic capture
mechanism_contract.subcategory_scope: General time tracking tools, automatic trackers, local activity loggers, and timer-based time trackers evaluated specifically for initiation reliability rather than billing depth, reporting breadth, or team administration.
mechanism_drift_risks: Treating any 'fast to use daily' comparison as if it proves no-manual-timer survival.
Confusing automatic background activity capture with complete project-ready timesheets.
Overstating mixed-mode tools such as Clockify, Paymo Track, or Timeular/EARLY as purely manual or purely automatic.
Using old Timeular hardware-only assumptions even though the current EARLY product also markets automated tracking.
Treating review-after-capture friction as the same thing as timer-initiation failure.

tools_that_can_be_named_if: Current evidence shows the tool survives because it captures activity passively or preserves a usable timeline without per-task manual initiation.
Current evidence shows the tool fails because default or outcome-dominant use still depends on remembering timer starts, stops, or switches.
For mixed-mode tools, the page copy is narrow enough to describe the specific mode being judged.
tools_that_should_not_be_named_if: The only support is the category page's editorial summary.
The evidence only proves general simplicity, daily speed, or billing precision rather than timer-initiation reliability.
Official product facts show both manual and automatic paths, but the page groups the tool absolutely without clarifying which mode is relevant.
required_evidence_for_survivor_group: Proof that activity capture happens automatically, passively, or with much lower initiation dependence in normal use.
Proof that the resulting record can be reviewed later without relying on the user's memory to recreate the day.
required_evidence_for_failure_group: Proof that normal use still depends on manual timer starts, stops, or deliberate switching interactions.
Proof that missing those initiation actions creates gaps or pushes the user into reconstruction later.

allowed_pairwise_evidence_sources: Time-tracking comparison pages whose decision rule explicitly turns on manual timer dependence versus automatic or passive capture.
Current category-gate evidence only when the gate reason itself is specifically manual-initiation friction rather than an adjacent mechanism.
weak_evidence_warning_conditions: The cited comparison belongs to time-scarcity, ceiling-check, or feature-aversion but only indirectly implies the manual-timer mechanism.
The tool has an automatic tracker mode in current product docs, but the page still groups it as a clean failure with no qualification.
The evidence item depends on physical-device interaction or general navigation friction rather than timer-initiation reliability specifically.
The gate verdict contradicts the category page claim.
